subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: Mean Value Theorem and Rolle's Theorem
hook: If you average 60 mph over a trip, at some instant your speedometer read exactly 60 — guaranteed, provable, no exceptions. The Mean Value Theorem turns that certainty into the most-cited theorem on the AP exam, and graders check its hypotheses like passport control.
learning_objectives: State Rolle's Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem with full hypotheses
Verify continuity and differentiability hypotheses explicitly before applying either theorem
Find the guaranteed c-values for given functions and intervals
Apply the MVT to real contexts: speed enforcement, table-based guarantees
Recognize hypothesis failures and construct or identify counterexamples

sections.title: Rolle's Theorem
sections.subtitle: Equal ends force a flat spot
sections.body:
Rolle's Theorem: if f is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b), then there exists at least one c in (a, b) with f'(c) = 0. A smooth curve that starts and ends at the same height must have a horizontal tangent somewhere in between — it either rises and comes back (a peak) or dips and returns (a valley) or stays flat (everywhere horizontal).

Each hypothesis earns its keep through counterexamples. Drop continuity: a function that jumps back to its start can avoid flat tangents. Drop differentiability: |x| on [-1, 1] has equal endpoint values but its only candidate flat spot is the corner at 0, where no derivative exists — the V never flattens. Drop equal endpoints: a straight ramp has no horizontal tangent. Three hypotheses, three counterexamples; the AP tests this correspondence directly.

The proof sketch is worth one read: a continuous function on a closed interval attains a maximum and minimum (the Extreme Value Theorem, next chapter). If both extremes occur at the endpoints, f is constant — every interior point works. Otherwise, an interior extreme exists, and interior extremes of differentiable functions have f' = 0 (Fermat's observation, also next chapter). Rolle is the bridge between those two facts.

Where Rolle works on the exam: 'show f'(c) = 0 for some c' problems, counting zeros of derivatives, and as the engine inside the MVT's proof. Pattern: verify the three hypotheses BY NAME, conclude with the theorem BY NAME, and report the interval where c lives.
key_terms: Continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), f(a) = f(b) ⟹ some c with f'(c) = 0
|x| (corner), jump functions, ramps — each kills one hypothesis and the conclusion
Verify each hypothesis explicitly, cite the theorem explicitly — the grading standard
boxes: ap_alert

Rolle and MVT justifications must name BOTH smoothness hypotheses: 'f is continuous on [1, 5] and differentiable on (1, 5).' Polynomials get the one-line certificate 'f is a polynomial, hence continuous and differentiable everywhere' — memorize that sentence; it appears in nearly every Unit 5 FRQ.

sections.title: The Mean Value Theorem
sections.subtitle: Somewhere, the instant matches the average
sections.body:
The Mean Value Theorem (MVT): if f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then some c in (a, b) satisfies f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a). In words: the instantaneous rate somewhere equals the average rate overall. Geometrically: some tangent line is parallel to the secant through the endpoints.

MVT is Rolle tilted. Subtract the secant line from f and the difference function has equal endpoint values (both zero) — Rolle applies, and the flat spot of the difference is exactly where f's tangent matches the secant's slope. Tilt Rolle's flat conclusion and you get MVT's parallel conclusion; the two theorems are one fact in two postures.

Finding the guaranteed c is a standard computation: for f(x) = x³ - 3x on [0, 3], the secant slope is (18 - 0)/3 = 6. Solve f'(c) = 6: 3c² - 3 = 6, c² = 3, c = √3 (the negative root lies outside the interval — discard it and SAY so). Answer: c = √3, in (0, 3). The discard step is graded; interval membership is part of the conclusion.

Note what MVT does NOT say: it does not locate c, does not promise uniqueness, and says nothing if the hypotheses fail. Like the IVT, it is an existence theorem — and the pair (IVT for values, MVT for rates) covers the AP's 'must there exist' questions almost completely: values between outputs route through IVT; rates between or equal to average rates route through MVT.
key_terms: Smooth on the interval ⟹ some c where f'(c) equals the average rate of change
The geometric reading: a tangent parallel to the endpoint secant
Compute the secant slope, solve f'(c) = it, discard roots outside (a, b) explicitly
boxes: ap_alert

'Must there exist a c with f'(c) = 4?' — compute the average rate first. If it equals 4 and the smoothness hypotheses hold, MVT says yes. If the average is NOT 4, the answer may still be yes via other reasoning (IVT on f', if f' is known continuous) — but MVT alone won't deliver it. Match the tool to the number.

sections.title: MVT in the Wild
sections.subtitle: Speeding tickets and table guarantees
sections.body:
The famous application: a car passes two toll cameras 30 miles apart, 24 minutes (0.4 hours) apart. Average speed: 75 mph. If the limit is 65, the MVT convicts: position is continuous and differentiable (cars don't teleport), so at some instant the speedometer read exactly 75 — over the limit, ticket justified. Several jurisdictions actually enforce this way; the calculus is airtight.

Table-based MVT: given a differentiable f with f(2) = 10 and f(6) = 30, some c in (2, 6) has f'(c) = 5. The exam stacks these — 'must there be a c in (1, 9) where f'(c) = 0?' — answered by finding two table entries with EQUAL values (Rolle through those points) or by applying MVT on subintervals and reasoning from the average rates. Differentiability hypotheses come from the stem ('f is differentiable on...'); cite them.

MVT also powers comparative bounds — the exam's sleeper question type: if f(0) = 3 and f'(x) ≤ 2 for all x, how large can f(5) be? By MVT on [0, 5], (f(5) - 3)/5 = f'(c) ≤ 2, so f(5) ≤ 13. Derivative bounds become function bounds through the theorem; no integration needed. The reverse direction (at least how big?) uses a lower bound on f' identically.

A hidden assumption to surface: applying MVT between table entries treats f as smooth BETWEEN samples — which the stem's 'differentiable' grants. Without that word, no guarantee survives. The discipline of checking who grants what, built through IVT and inverse functions, continues to pay.
key_terms: Average speed over the limit ⟹ instantaneous speed over the limit somewhere (MVT)
Two equal table values + differentiability ⟹ f' = 0 between them
f' ≤ M on [a,b] ⟹ f(b) ≤ f(a) + M(b - a) — derivative bounds become value bounds
boxes: ap_alert

Bound-propagation questions ('what is the maximum possible value of f(5)?') are MVT in disguise and appear on BC exams regularly. The three-line answer: MVT gives (f(5) - f(0))/5 = f'(c); f'(c) ≤ 2; solve. Recognize the disguise and the question is routine.

sections.title: Hypothesis Forensics
sections.subtitle: When theorems don't apply
sections.body:
The exam tests hypothesis failure as often as application. f(x) = 1/x on [-1, 1]: f(-1) = -1, f(1) = 1, average rate 1 — yet f'(x) = -1/x² is NEGATIVE everywhere it exists. No c matches. No contradiction: f is discontinuous at 0, inside the interval; MVT never promised anything. Spotting the failed hypothesis IS the answer to such problems.

f(x) = |x| on [-1, 2]: continuous everywhere, but not differentiable at 0 ∈ (-1, 2). Here the average rate is (2 - 1)/3 = 1/3, while f' takes only the values ±1 wherever it exists — never 1/3, so the MVT's conclusion genuinely fails. One interior corner is enough to void the warranty. The hypotheses are not legal boilerplate; they are load-bearing.

The corrected instinct: when asked 'does the MVT apply?', check continuity on the CLOSED interval, differentiability on the OPEN interval — endpoints may be corner-free zones — and answer with the specific failure or the specific certification. 'Does not apply because f is not differentiable at x = 0, which is in (-1, 2)' is a complete, full-credit answer.

Forensics extends to converse abuse: f'(c) equaling the average rate at some c does NOT certify the hypotheses held (plenty of broken functions accidentally satisfy the conclusion). Like IVT's false converse, the implication runs one way. Theorems are one-way streets, and the exam's 'which must be true' questions are built on students driving them backward.
key_terms: Identify the specific broken hypothesis and its location — that IS the answer
One non-differentiable interior point voids MVT, even with continuity everywhere
The conclusion holding accidentally does not resurrect failed hypotheses
boxes: ap_alert

For 'does MVT apply?' questions, the answer template is: 'No — f is not [continuous/differentiable] at x = [point], which lies in the interval.' Name the property AND the point. Vague answers ('f isn't smooth enough') earn nothing.

mcq.question: f(x) = x² - 4x + 1 on [0, 4]. The c guaranteed by Rolle's Theorem is
mcq.explanation: f(0) = f(4) = 1, polynomial smoothness holds: f'(c) = 2c - 4 = 0 gives c = 2.

mcq.question: f(x) = x³ on [0, 2]. The c guaranteed by the MVT satisfies
mcq.explanation: Average rate: 8/2 = 4. Solve 3c² = 4: c = 2/√3 ≈ 1.155, inside (0, 2).

mcq.question: A trucker's logbook shows 140 miles covered in 2 hours on a highway with a 65 mph limit. The MVT guarantees

choices.A: the truck's speed was exactly 70 mph at some instant
choices.C: the truck's average speed equals its final speed

mcq.explanation: Average speed 70 mph; position is continuous and differentiable, so some instant's speedometer read exactly 70 — incidentally proving a violation.

mcq.question: For f(x) = |x - 1| on [0, 3], the MVT conclusion fails because

choices.B: f is not differentiable at x = 1, which is in (0, 3)
choices.D: the average rate of change is zero

mcq.explanation: The corner at x = 1 sits inside the open interval, voiding the differentiability hypothesis. (Continuity holds; equal endpoints are Rolle's requirement, not MVT's.)

mcq.question: f is differentiable everywhere with f(1) = 5 and f'(x) ≤ 3 for all x. The largest possible value of f(4) is

frq.question:
Let f(x) = x³ - 6x² + 9x + 2 on the interval [0, 4].
(a) Verify that the hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem hold, and compute the average rate of change of f on [0, 4].
(b) Find all values of c guaranteed by the MVT.
(c) Separately, verify that Rolle's Theorem applies to f on [1, 3], and find its guaranteed c.
rubric: (a) Polynomial ⟹ continuous on [0,4], differentiable on (0,4); average rate = (f(4) - f(0))/4 = (6 - 2)/4 = 1
(c) Evaluates f(1) = 6 and f(3) = 2; since they are unequal, identifies that Rolle's equal-endpoint hypothesis fails on [1, 3]
Correct handling of the discard/verification logic in each part
frq.model_answer: (a) f is a polynomial, hence continuous on [0, 4] and differentiable on (0, 4). f(0) = 2, f(4) = 64 - 96 + 36 + 2 = 6: average rate = (6 - 2)/4 = 1. (b) Solve 3c² - 12c + 9 = 1: 3c² - 12c + 8 = 0, c = (12 ± √(144 - 96))/6 = 2 ± (2√3)/3 ≈ 0.845 and 3.155 — both inside (0, 4), so both are guaranteed values. (c) Check the endpoint values: f(1) = 1 - 6 + 9 + 2 = 6 and f(3) = 27 - 54 + 27 + 2 = 2. Since f(1) ≠ f(3), Rolle's equal-endpoint hypothesis fails on [1, 3] and the theorem does not apply there. (MVT still applies, with average rate (2 - 6)/2 = -2.)

frq.question:
A differentiable function g satisfies the table: g(0) = 4, g(2) = 10, g(5) = 10, g(8) = -2.
(a) Must there exist a c in (0, 8) with g'(c) = 0? Justify with the appropriate theorem.
(b) Must there exist a c in (0, 8) with g'(c) = -4? Justify.
(c) Can g'(x) > 0 for all x in (5, 8)? Explain.
rubric: (a) Yes: g(2) = g(5) = 10 with g differentiable ⟹ Rolle on [2, 5] gives c in (2, 5) ⊂ (0, 8)
(b) Yes: MVT on [5, 8] gives average rate (-2 - 10)/3 = -4, so some c in (5, 8) has g'(c) = -4
(c) No: by MVT the average rate on (5,8) is -4 < 0, so g' takes a negative value there
Hypotheses (differentiable, hence continuous) cited in each part
frq.model_answer: (a) Yes. g is differentiable (hence continuous), and g(2) = g(5) = 10. By Rolle's Theorem on [2, 5], some c in (2, 5) has g'(c) = 0 — and (2, 5) ⊂ (0, 8). (b) Yes. By the MVT on [5, 8]: some c in (5, 8) satisfies g'(c) = (g(8) - g(5))/(8 - 5) = (-2 - 10)/3 = -4. (c) No. Part (b) produced a point in (5, 8) where g' = -4 < 0, so g' cannot be positive throughout that interval — the function must fall on net from 10 to -2, and the MVT pins an instant of negative rate.

frq.question:
Let f(x) = x^{2/3} on the interval [-8, 8].
(a) Show that f(-8) = f(8), and compute f'(x) where it exists.
(b) Show that there is NO c in (-8, 8) with f'(c) = 0.
(c) Reconcile (a) and (b) with Rolle's Theorem — why is there no contradiction?
rubric: (b) f'(x) = 2/(3x^{1/3}) is never zero (numerator constant 2)
(c) f is not differentiable at x = 0 (cusp), which lies in (-8, 8)
Concludes Rolle's differentiability hypothesis fails, so its conclusion is not guaranteed
frq.model_answer: (a) f(-8) = (-8)^{2/3} = 4 and f(8) = 4 — equal. For x ≠ 0, f'(x) = (2/3)x^{-1/3}. (b) f'(x) = 2/(3x^{1/3}) has constant numerator 2, so it never equals zero anywhere it exists. (c) Rolle's Theorem requires differentiability on the whole open interval, but f has a cusp at x = 0 ∈ (-8, 8) (one-sided difference quotients blow up to opposite infinities). With a failed hypothesis, the theorem promises nothing — equal endpoints without a flat tangent is perfectly consistent, and f's V-like cusp at the origin is exactly the shape that does it.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: Extreme Value Theorem and Critical Points
hook: Optimization starts with a hunting license: where CAN a maximum hide? The answer — only at critical points or endpoints — shrinks an infinite search to a short list you can check by hand. This chapter issues the license.
learning_objectives: State the Extreme Value Theorem and the role of its closed-interval hypothesis
Define critical points: f'(c) = 0 or f'(c) undefined, with c in the domain
Find all critical points across polynomial, rational, radical, and trig functions
Execute the closed-interval (candidates) test for absolute extrema
Distinguish critical points from extrema — the location list versus the verdicts

sections.title: The Extreme Value Theorem
sections.subtitle: Closed and continuous means extremes exist
sections.body:
The Extreme Value Theorem (EVT): a function continuous on a CLOSED interval [a, b] attains an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on that interval. Existence, guaranteed — before any computation, you know the search has a quarry. Like IVT and MVT, the theorem is silent about WHERE; it only rules out the hunt being futile.

Both hypotheses are load-bearing. Open intervals lose the guarantee: f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1) climbs without bound (no max) and slides toward 1 without reaching it (no min attained). Discontinuity loses it too: a function jumping just below its would-be peak never attains a maximum. The standard counterexample pair — open interval, jump discontinuity — answers every 'why closed? why continuous?' exam prompt.

EVT's role in the architecture: it powers Rolle (whose proof needed extremes to exist), it justifies the closed-interval test (the section after next), and it underwrites every applied optimization that ends '...so the maximum exists and equals the largest candidate.' The theorem rarely stars in its own question; it is cited in the supporting role constantly.

The statement's precision matters on multiple choice: EVT promises the extreme VALUES are attained at points of the interval — possibly at endpoints, possibly at several points, possibly with max = min (constant functions). What it never promises: interior locations, uniqueness, or anything off a closed interval.
key_terms: Continuous on [a, b] ⟹ absolute max and min are attained on [a, b]
Open interval (1/x on (0,1)) and a jump function — each kills one hypothesis
EVT certifies existence so the candidates test's comparison is decisive
boxes: ap_alert

EVT applies to closed intervals ONLY. 'Find the absolute maximum of f on (0, ∞)' carries no EVT guarantee — such problems need limit analysis at the open ends to confirm the interior candidate wins. Check the interval's brackets before assuming extremes exist.

sections.title: Critical Points
sections.subtitle: Where extremes are allowed to happen
sections.body:
A critical point of f is an interior domain point c where f'(c) = 0 OR f'(c) does not exist. Fermat's theorem supplies the why: if f has a local extreme at an interior point where f is differentiable, then f'(c) = 0 — a nonzero slope means the function is actively rising or falling through c, so c cannot be a peak or valley. Add the points where f' fails to exist (corners, cusps, vertical tangents — extremes can hide there too, as |x|'s minimum at its corner shows), and the list of POSSIBLE interior extreme locations is complete.

Finding critical points is a two-part hunt: solve f'(x) = 0, and separately list domain points where f' is undefined. For f(x) = x^{2/3}(x - 5) = x^{5/3} - 5x^{2/3}: f'(x) = (5/3)x^{2/3} - (10/3)x^{-1/3} = (5/3)x^{-1/3}(x - 2). Zero at x = 2; undefined at x = 0 (which IS in f's domain). Two critical points, two different species — and forgetting the undefined-derivative species is the classic omission.

Domain membership is non-negotiable: f(x) = 1/x has f'(x) = -1/x², undefined at 0 — but 0 is not in f's domain, so it is NOT a critical point (it is a vertical asymptote, a different beast). The checklist: c must be in the domain of f, and f'(c) must be zero or nonexistent.

Vocabulary precision for the exam: critical points are CANDIDATES, not winners. f(x) = x³ has a critical point at 0 (f' = 3x² = 0) but no extreme there — the curve pauses and continues rising. The next two chapters build the verdict machinery (first and second derivative tests); this chapter only assembles the suspect list.
key_terms: Interior domain point with f'(c) = 0 or f'(c) undefined
Interior extremes of differentiable functions occur only where f' = 0
x³ at 0: critical point, no extreme — tests come later
boxes: ap_alert

The two-species hunt is graded: 'find all critical points' answers missing the f'-undefined points (cusps of x^{2/3}-type functions) lose half the credit. Any function with fractional exponents or absolute values should trigger the undefined-derivative check.

sections.title: The Closed-Interval Test
sections.subtitle: Candidates, evaluate, compare
sections.body:
For absolute extrema of a continuous f on [a, b], the candidates test: (1) find all critical points in (a, b); (2) evaluate f at each critical point AND at both endpoints; (3) the largest value is the absolute max, the smallest the absolute min. EVT guarantees winners exist; Fermat guarantees no interior point outside the list can win; the comparison crowns them.

Worked: f(x) = x³ - 12x on [0, 3]. f'(x) = 3x² - 12 = 0 at x = ±2; only 2 lies in (0, 3). Evaluate: f(0) = 0, f(2) = -16, f(3) = -9. Absolute max 0 (at x = 0), absolute min -16 (at x = 2). Note the max landed on an ENDPOINT — endpoints win often, and forgetting to evaluate them is the test's most common fumble.

Answer-reporting precision: 'the absolute maximum VALUE is 0, attained at x = 0.' Exam questions ask for the value, the location, or both — read which. A table presentation (x-candidates in one column, f-values in the next) is self-organizing, grader-friendly, and prevents the evaluate-the-wrong-function slip of plugging candidates into f' instead of f.

The test needs NO derivative-sign analysis, no concavity, no classification machinery — brute comparison wins on closed intervals. Save the fancier tests for open intervals and local questions where comparison lists don't close. Matching method to question type — closed-interval test here, derivative tests there — is itself a tested skill.
key_terms: Critical points + endpoints, evaluate f at each, compare — done
Endpoints win frequently; they are mandatory candidates
The comparison runs on FUNCTION values; plugging into f' is the classic slip
boxes: ap_alert

Present the candidates test as a small table: candidate x | f(x). The table format guarantees you evaluated the right function at every candidate and lets the grader award points at a glance. Free organization, free accuracy.

sections.title: Local versus Absolute
sections.subtitle: Two questions, two toolkits
sections.body:
Absolute (global) extremes are champions over the WHOLE domain or interval; local (relative) extremes are champions of a neighborhood — the peaks and valleys of the landscape, whether or not they are the highest peak or lowest valley. Every interior absolute extreme is local, but local extremes are usually not absolute. The distinction routes method selection: absolute on a closed interval → candidates test; local anywhere → derivative-sign tests (next chapters).

Endpoint subtlety: by the AP's convention, endpoints CAN host absolute extremes (the candidates test includes them) and are generally not classified as local extremes — local-ness requires an open neighborhood inside the domain on both sides. Exam questions avoid punishing this edge case, but the candidates test's inclusion of endpoints is exactly how absolute questions stay safe.

Reading questions for the routing keywords: 'absolute maximum on [1, 5]' → candidates test. 'Relative minimum' → first/second derivative test. 'Maximum value of f' with no interval — check whether the domain is naturally closed or whether limit analysis at infinity is needed. The keyword-to-method map prevents the standard mismatch errors (running sign analysis when comparison suffices, or comparing endpoint values when the question wanted a local classification).

The unit ahead, mapped from here: Chapter 3 classifies critical points by f's increasing/decreasing pattern (first derivative test); Chapter 4 classifies by concavity (second derivative test); Chapter 5 assembles full curve sketches; Chapter 6 optimizes applied quantities — where the candidates list and the classification tests do their real work. The suspect list from this chapter feeds everything.
key_terms: Closed-interval absolute → candidates test; local classification → derivative tests
Endpoints join absolute comparisons; local extremes live at interior points
boxes: ap_alert

'Absolute' + closed interval = candidates test, no sign charts needed. 'Relative/local' = sign analysis, no endpoint comparison needed. Mixing the toolkits wastes exam minutes — the question's adjective picks the tool.

mcq.question: The critical points of f(x) = x³ - 3x² - 9x + 1 are
mcq.explanation: f'(x) = 3x² - 6x - 9 = 3(x - 3)(x + 1) = 0 at x = -1, 3; f' exists everywhere.

mcq.question: f(x) = x^{2/3} has a critical point at x = 0 because

choices.B: f'(0) does not exist and 0 is in the domain
choices.D: the graph crosses the x-axis there

mcq.explanation: f'(x) = (2/3)x^{-1/3} blows up at 0, but f(0) = 0 is defined — the undefined-derivative species of critical point (a cusp).

mcq.question: The absolute maximum of f(x) = x³ - 3x on [0, 2] is
mcq.explanation: Critical point in (0,2): x = 1 (f' = 3x² - 3). Candidates: f(0) = 0, f(1) = -2, f(2) = 2. Largest: 2.

mcq.question: Which function fails to attain an absolute maximum on the given set?
mcq.explanation: On [0, 1), f grows without bound as x → 1⁻ — the interval isn't closed, so EVT doesn't apply and no max is attained.

mcq.question: f'(c) = 0 at an interior point c. Which statement MUST be true?

choices.A: f has a local extreme at c
choices.B: c is a critical point of f
choices.C: f has an absolute extreme at c

mcq.explanation: Zero derivative makes c a critical point by definition — but only a candidate: x³ at 0 shows the extreme and direction-change claims can fail.

frq.question:
Let f(x) = x⁴ - 8x² + 3 on the interval [-1, 3].
(a) Find all critical points of f in the open interval (-1, 3).
(b) Apply the candidates test to find the absolute maximum and minimum values of f on [-1, 3], presenting your evaluations in a table.
(c) State where each absolute extreme is attained, and identify which candidates were critical points versus endpoints.
rubric: (c) Absolute max 12 at x = 3 (endpoint); absolute min -13 at x = 2 (critical point)
Discards x = -2 as outside the interval, explicitly
frq.model_answer: (a) f'(x) = 4x³ - 16x = 4x(x² - 4) = 4x(x - 2)(x + 2). Zeros: x = -2, 0, 2; only x = 0 and x = 2 lie in (-1, 3) (x = -2 is outside — discarded). (b) Candidates table: x = -1: f = 1 - 8 + 3 = -4; x = 0: f = 3; x = 2: f = 16 - 32 + 3 = -13; x = 3: f = 81 - 72 + 3 = 12. (c) The absolute maximum value is 12, attained at the endpoint x = 3; the absolute minimum value is -13, attained at the critical point x = 2. (EVT guaranteed both exist: f is a polynomial, continuous on the closed interval.)

frq.question:
Let g(x) = x^{2/3}(x - 5), defined for all real x.
(a) Show that g'(x) = (5/3)x^{-1/3}(x - 2), and find all critical points of g.
(b) Find the absolute extremes of g on [-1, 8] using the candidates test.
(c) One of your critical points is a cusp. Identify it, and explain how a point with no derivative can still host an extreme.
rubric: (a) Product/power computation to the given form; critical points x = 2 (zero) and x = 0 (undefined, in domain)
Absolute max 12 at x = 8; absolute min -6 at x = -1
(c) x = 0 is the cusp; extremes need only a neighborhood comparison, not a slope — |x|'s corner-minimum analogy
frq.model_answer: (a) g(x) = x^{5/3} - 5x^{2/3}, so g'(x) = (5/3)x^{2/3} - (10/3)x^{-1/3} = (5/3)x^{-1/3}(x - 2). Critical points: g' = 0 at x = 2; g' undefined at x = 0, which is in g's domain — both are critical points. (b) Candidates: g(-1) = (1)(-6) = -6; g(0) = 0; g(2) = 2^{2/3}(-3) ≈ -4.762; g(8) = 4(3) = 12. Absolute maximum 12 at x = 8 (endpoint); absolute minimum -6 at x = -1 (endpoint). (c) The cusp is x = 0: one-sided slopes blow up oppositely. An extreme is a statement about VALUES — g(0) ≥ g(x) nearby or not — and needs no tangent line. The function |x| has its minimum at a corner for the same reason; smoothness is sufficient machinery for FINDING extremes, never a prerequisite for HAVING them.

frq.question:
A function h is continuous on [0, 10] with h'(x) = (x - 3)²(x - 7) for 0 < x < 10.
(a) Find all critical points of h in (0, 10).
(b) Without evaluating h, determine which critical point(s) could host a local extreme, by examining the sign of h' on each side. (A full classification chapter follows; use sign reasoning directly.)
(c) Where must the absolute minimum of h on [0, 10] occur? Justify using your sign analysis and the candidates principle.
rubric: (a) h' = 0 at x = 3 and x = 7
(b) (x-3)² ≥ 0 always: h' sign is the sign of (x - 7): negative on (0,3)∪(3,7), positive on (7,10); only x = 7 has a sign change
(c) h decreases on (0, 7), increases on (7, 10): minimum at x = 7
Justification: endpoints are higher (h falls to 7 and rises after), so the interior sign-change point wins
frq.model_answer: (a) h'(x) = (x - 3)²(x - 7) = 0 at x = 3 and x = 7 — both in (0, 10), both critical points. (b) The factor (x - 3)² is nonnegative, so the sign of h' matches the sign of (x - 7): h' < 0 on (0, 3) and (3, 7); h' > 0 on (7, 10). At x = 3 there is NO sign change (negative on both sides) — no extreme; at x = 7 the sign flips from − to +: a local minimum candidate confirmed. (c) h decreases across (0, 7) (the touch-and-continue at 3 notwithstanding) and increases on (7, 10). So h(7) is below every other value: h(0) > h(7) and h(10) > h(7). The absolute minimum on [0, 10] occurs at x = 7.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: First Derivative Test and Function Behavior
hook: A sign chart of f' is an X-ray of f: where the derivative is positive the function climbs, where negative it falls, and every sign flip marks a peak or a valley. One chart, drawn once, answers half the questions on any Unit 5 free response.
learning_objectives: Determine intervals of increase and decrease from the sign of f'
Construct accurate sign charts using critical points as boundaries
Apply the First Derivative Test to classify critical points
Write interval-and-sign justifications in the AP's graded format
Analyze functions given f' as a graph or formula without knowing f

sections.title: Increasing, Decreasing, and the Sign of f'
sections.subtitle: The fundamental correspondence
sections.body:
If f' > 0 on an interval, f is increasing there; f' < 0, decreasing. The MVT proves it: for any two points x₁ < x₂ in the interval, f(x₂) - f(x₁) = f'(c)(x₂ - x₁) for some c between them, and a positive f'(c) forces the difference positive. The previous chapter's theorem quietly underwrites this one — the logical chain EVT → Rolle → MVT → increasing/decreasing is the unit's spine.

The sign of f' can only change where f' is zero or undefined — at critical points (or discontinuities of f). So critical points partition the domain into intervals of constant f'-sign, and ONE test value per interval determines the sign throughout. That is the entire sign-chart algorithm: mark the critical points, test one point per gap, record the signs.

Worked: f(x) = x³ - 3x² - 9x + 4. f'(x) = 3(x² - 2x - 3) = 3(x - 3)(x + 1). Critical points -1, 3 split the line into three intervals. Test x = -2: f' = 3(-5)(-1) > 0. Test 0: 3(-3)(1) < 0. Test 4: 3(1)(5) > 0. Chart: + − +. Conclusion: f increases on (-∞, -1), decreases on (-1, 3), increases on (3, ∞).

Interval-notation care: the AP accepts open or closed interval answers for increasing/decreasing (both conventions appear in textbooks), but consistency and correct boundary identification are graded. The safe standard: report open intervals bounded by the critical points, and never union across a critical point where the sign changes.
key_terms: f' > 0 ⟹ increasing; f' < 0 ⟹ decreasing — proved by MVT
Critical points partition; one test value per interval settles each sign
Signs can flip only at critical points or discontinuities — nowhere else
boxes: ap_alert

Justifications must reference f', not the graph's looks: 'f is increasing on (3, ∞) BECAUSE f'(x) > 0 there.' The because-clause with the derivative's sign is the graded unit; conclusions without it score zero on justification points.

sections.title: The First Derivative Test
sections.subtitle: Sign flips classify critical points
sections.body:
The First Derivative Test (1DT): at a critical point c, if f' changes from + to −, f has a local MAXIMUM at c (rising then falling — a peak); from − to +, a local MINIMUM (falling then rising — a valley); no sign change, NO extreme (the function pauses and resumes its direction — x³'s flat crossing at 0).

The test reads straight off the sign chart. From the worked example (+ − + with critical points -1 and 3): at x = -1, + flips to −: local max. At x = 3, − flips to +: local min. The chart built for increasing/decreasing intervals classifies the critical points for free — one artifact, two question types answered, which is why building the chart FIRST is the standing strategy.

The no-change case is the exam's favorite subtlety, engineered by squared factors: f'(x) = (x - 3)²(x - 7) from last chapter's FRQ has a critical point at 3 with NO extreme (the square keeps f' negative on both sides). Squared factors in f' are flags: expect a touch-without-flip at those roots. Cusps classify too: x^{2/3} has f' undefined at 0, with sign − then + around it — a local minimum at a point with no derivative, the 1DT handling what the (coming) second derivative test cannot.

Justification grammar, graded verbatim: 'f has a local maximum at x = -1 because f' changes sign from positive to negative at x = -1.' The CHANGE language is essential — citing f'(-1) = 0 alone classifies nothing (x³ warns why). State the flip, earn the point.
key_terms: +→− max; −→+ min; no change, no extreme
Even powers in f' mark critical points without sign changes
The justification cites the SIGN CHANGE, never just f'(c) = 0
boxes: ap_alert

The 1DT works at critical points where f' is UNDEFINED (cusps, corners) — places the second derivative test cannot touch. When a function has fractional exponents or absolute values, the 1DT is not just sufficient but mandatory.

sections.title: Working from f' Alone
sections.subtitle: The graph-of-the-derivative genre
sections.body:
The AP's signature Unit 5 genre: you are shown the GRAPH of f' (not f!) and asked about f. Every question routes through one translation: heights of the f'-graph are slopes of f. Where the f'-graph is ABOVE the axis, f increases. Where the f'-graph CROSSES the axis downward (+ to −), f has a local max. The f'-graph's own peaks and valleys are NOT extremes of f — they will matter next chapter (they mark inflection points of f).

The discipline is resisting the reflex to treat the displayed curve as f. Students who annotate the printout — writing 'this is f-PRIME' at the top, marking axis crossings with 'CP' and labeling each region + or − — convert the genre into the familiar sign-chart workflow. The graph IS a sign chart, drawn fancy.

Typical question battery for an f'-graph with zeros at 1, 4, 6 (crossing down, touching, crossing up respectively): Where is f increasing? (Wherever f' ≥ 0: read the above-axis intervals.) Local extremes? (Max at 1, nothing at 4 — a touch, not a cross — min at 6.) Where is f' itself decreasing? (Different question! Read the f'-graph's own downhill stretches.) The battery's danger is question (3)-type switches — about f' as a function rather than as f's slope — and the cure is reading each prompt's subject noun slowly.

Given numerical f' formulas with no closed form for f (like f'(x) = e^{-x²} - 0.5), calculator-active versions run the same logic: graph f', find its zeros numerically, classify by the crossing direction. The translation skill — heights to slopes, crossings to extremes — is identical across presentation formats, and it is the single most leveraged skill in the unit.
key_terms: The f'-graph's y-values are f's slopes — the genre's one translation rule
Axis crossings of f' flip f's direction; touches do not
'Where is f' decreasing?' asks about the displayed curve itself — watch the prompt switch
boxes: ap_alert

First move on any graph-of-f' problem: write 'THIS IS f′' above the figure and mark each axis crossing. The 15-second annotation prevents the single most common Unit 5 error — answering about the displayed curve when asked about f.

sections.title: Behavior Synthesis
sections.subtitle: From sign data to function portraits
sections.body:
Sign charts compose into qualitative portraits. From + − + with critical points -1 and 3, and values f(-1) = 9, f(3) = -23: the function climbs to a peak of 9 at x = -1, descends through the midzone to a valley of -23 at 3, then climbs away. Add end behavior (a positive cubic: −∞ to ∞) and the portrait is complete enough to sketch — which is precisely Chapter 5's program, with concavity refinements from Chapter 4.

Monotonicity consequences feed other question types. A function increasing on an entire interval is one-to-one there — invertibility certificates from Unit 3 reappear ('f' > 0 everywhere ⟹ f has an inverse'). Roots count via monotonicity too: a continuous function increasing through a sign change crosses zero EXACTLY once on that stretch — IVT gives at-least-one, monotonicity gives at-most-one. The 'exactly one root' FRQ is this pair, cited in sequence.

Motion reprise: a particle's 'moving right' intervals are v > 0 readings on v's sign chart — the same chart, the same flips, with turnarounds at v's sign changes. Unit 4's motion analysis was this chapter's machinery applied to s'; recognizing the identity means motion problems cost no new study.

The chapter's deliverable, stated plainly: given any f (formula, f'-graph, or table of f'-signs), produce the increasing/decreasing intervals, the classified critical points, and the justification sentences, in under five minutes. That deliverable plus concavity (next) IS the AP's curve-analysis question. Drill the chart; the rest is reading it.
key_terms: Signs + critical values + end behavior = a sketchable description of f
IVT (at least one) + monotonicity (at most one), cited together
Direction analysis is the 1DT applied to v = s' — the same chart
boxes: ap_alert

'Show f has exactly one zero in [a, b]' is a two-theorem sandwich: IVT for existence (sign change at the ends, continuity), then 'f' > 0 throughout, so f is increasing and cannot return to zero' for uniqueness. Both halves must appear; each carries points.

frq.question:
Let f(x) = 3x⁴ - 8x³ - 6x² + 24x.
(a) Compute f'(x) and factor it completely. (It factors with integer roots.)
(b) Build the sign chart for f' and state the intervals where f is increasing and decreasing.
(c) Classify every critical point using the First Derivative Test, with the standard justification sentences.
rubric: (b) Signs on (-∞,-1), (-1,1), (1,2), (2,∞): − + − +; increasing on (-1,1) and (2,∞), decreasing elsewhere
(c) x = -1: − to + local min; x = 1: + to − local max; x = 2: − to + local min
Justifications cite the sign changes explicitly
frq.model_answer: (a) f'(x) = 12x³ - 24x² - 12x + 24 = 12(x³ - 2x² - x + 2) = 12[x²(x - 2) - (x - 2)] = 12(x - 2)(x² - 1) = 12(x - 2)(x - 1)(x + 1). (b) Test values give the chart − + − + across the critical points -1, 1, 2: f is increasing on (-1, 1) and (2, ∞); decreasing on (-∞, -1) and (1, 2). (c) At x = -1, f' changes from negative to positive: local minimum. At x = 1, f' changes from positive to negative: local maximum. At x = 2, f' changes from negative to positive: local minimum. Each conclusion follows from the First Derivative Test via the stated sign change.

frq.question:
The figure (described): the graph of f', the DERIVATIVE of f, on [0, 9]. It is positive on (0, 2), crosses zero downward at x = 2, negative on (2, 5), touches zero at x = 5 without crossing, negative on (5, 8), and crosses upward at x = 8.
(a) On what intervals is f increasing? Justify.
(b) Find and classify all local extremes of f in (0, 9).
(c) A student claims f has a local minimum at x = 5 'because f' is zero there.' Explain the error with a justification the student should have written.
rubric: (a) f increasing on (0, 2) and (8, 9), where f' > 0
(b) Local max at x = 2 (+ to −); local min at x = 8 (− to +); nothing at x = 5
(c) f'(5) = 0 alone classifies nothing; the sign does not change at 5 (negative both sides)
Correct justification: no sign change ⟹ no extreme — f merely pauses while decreasing
frq.model_answer: (a) f is increasing exactly where its derivative is positive: on (0, 2) and (8, 9). (b) At x = 2, f' crosses from + to −: local maximum. At x = 8, f' crosses from − to +: local minimum. At x = 5, f' touches zero but stays negative on both sides: no extreme. (c) The student used the wrong criterion: f'(c) = 0 makes c a CANDIDATE, not a winner. Classification requires a sign change, and here f' is negative on (2, 5) and on (5, 8) alike — f decreases, pauses momentarily at 5, and continues decreasing. The correct sentence: 'f has no local extreme at x = 5 because f' does not change sign there.'

frq.question:
Let g(x) = x - 2 sin x on the interval [0, 2π].
(a) Find all critical points of g in (0, 2π).
(b) Determine the intervals of increase and decrease.
(c) Show that g has exactly one zero in the interval (π/3, π), citing both theorems your argument needs.
rubric: (a) g' = 1 - 2cos x = 0: cos x = 1/2, x = π/3 and 5π/3
(c) g(π/3) = π/3 - √3 < 0, g(π) = π > 0: IVT gives a zero; g' > 0 on the interval gives uniqueness
Both theorem citations (IVT, monotonicity via positive derivative) present
frq.model_answer: (a) g'(x) = 1 - 2cos x = 0 when cos x = 1/2: x = π/3 and x = 5π/3. (b) cos x > 1/2 on (0, π/3) makes g' < 0 (decreasing); cos x < 1/2 on (π/3, 5π/3) makes g' > 0 (increasing); cos x > 1/2 again on (5π/3, 2π): decreasing. (c) g is continuous; g(π/3) = π/3 - 2(√3/2) = π/3 - √3 ≈ -0.685 < 0, and g(π) = π - 0 > 0. By the IVT, g has at least one zero in (π/3, π). On that interval g' = 1 - 2cos x > 0 (it lies inside (π/3, 5π/3)), so g is strictly increasing there and can cross zero at most once. Exactly one zero.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: Concavity and the Second Derivative Test
hook: Two roads can both climb — but one bends upward, accelerating, while the other bends over, exhausting itself. Concavity is the bend, f'' is its detector, and inflection points mark where the bending flips. This is the layer that turns sign charts into true portraits.
learning_objectives: Define concavity via the behavior of f' and detect it with the sign of f''
Find inflection points, verifying the concavity change rather than just f'' = 0
Apply the Second Derivative Test to classify critical points
Choose between the first and second derivative tests, knowing when 2DT is silent
Connect concavity to tangent-line position and estimation error directions

sections.title: What Concavity Is
sections.subtitle: The slope's own trend
sections.body:
A graph is concave UP on an interval when its slope is increasing there — tangent lines rotate counterclockwise as you move right, and the curve sits ABOVE every tangent it owns, cupping upward. Concave DOWN: slopes decreasing, curve below its tangents, capping over. The official detector: f'' > 0 means f' increasing means concave up; f'' < 0, concave down.

Concavity is independent of increasing/decreasing — the four combinations all exist and all matter. Rising concave-up (accelerating growth: early exponential), rising concave-down (saturating growth: filling tank), falling concave-up (decelerating decline: cooling coffee), falling concave-down (accelerating decline: early free fall measured downward). The 2×2 grid of (f' sign, f'' sign) is the complete local taxonomy, and 'sketch a curve that is decreasing and concave up' is a real exam instruction.

Precision note: concavity describes f' 's MONOTONICITY, so the honest definition is 'f' increasing' — detectable by f'' > 0 when f'' exists, but meaningful even where it doesn't. For AP purposes, the f''-sign criterion is the working tool, with the f'-increasing language as the deeper justification accepted equally by rubrics.

The tangent-position consequence already earned its keep in linearization: concave up puts curves above tangents (underestimates), concave down below (overestimates). Euler's method and Taylor polynomial error directions — both BC staples — run on the same geometry. One picture, four units of applications.
key_terms: f' increasing (f'' > 0): curve above its tangents, cupping
f' decreasing (f'' < 0): curve below its tangents, capping
(f' sign, f'' sign) pairs: the four local shapes every curve is built from
boxes: ap_alert

'Increasing at a decreasing rate' (f' > 0, f'' < 0) and its three siblings appear constantly in applied stems. Translate prose to the sign pair FIRST, then reason. The 2×2 grid taped to your mental wall is worth several points a year.

sections.title: Inflection Points
sections.subtitle: Where the bend flips
sections.body:
An inflection point is a point on the graph where concavity CHANGES — cup to cap or cap to cup. Detection mirrors critical points one derivative up: candidates are where f'' = 0 or f'' is undefined; winners are candidates where f'' actually changes sign. The verification step is non-optional: f(x) = x⁴ has f''(0) = 0 but f'' = 12x² ≥ 0 on both sides — no sign change, no inflection, the curve stays cupped.

Worked: f(x) = x³ - 6x² + 9x. f''(x) = 6x - 12, zero at x = 2, sign − then +: concavity flips from down to up at x = 2 — inflection point at (2, f(2)) = (2, 2). Report inflection points as POINTS (both coordinates) when asked for points; x-values alone when asked where.

On the graph of f', inflection points of f appear as local extremes of f' — where the slope stops increasing and starts decreasing (or vice versa). This completes last chapter's translation table: f'-graph crossings ↔ f's extremes; f'-graph extremes ↔ f's inflections. The graph-of-f' genre tests both rows, usually in the same problem.

Inflection points carry applied meaning: the steepest point of a logistic curve (epidemic's fastest-spread day, product adoption's peak velocity) is an inflection — growth still positive but switching from accelerating to decelerating. 'When is the rate of change greatest?' on a rising S-curve is an inflection question, and Unit 7's logistic differential equation returns here for its famous P = L/2 moment.
key_terms: A point where concavity changes — f'' flips sign there
f'' = 0 without a sign change is no inflection — verify the flip
Extremes of the f'-graph are inflection points of f
boxes: ap_alert
Inflection justifications are graded like 1DT ones: 'f has an inflection point at x = 2 because f'' changes sign there.' Citing f''(2) = 0 alone fails (x⁴!). Same grammar, one derivative higher.

sections.title: The Second Derivative Test
sections.subtitle: Concavity classifies critical points
sections.body:
The Second Derivative Test (2DT): suppose f'(c) = 0. If f''(c) > 0, the curve is cupped at a flat point — local MINIMUM. If f''(c) < 0, capped at a flat point — local MAXIMUM. If f''(c) = 0, the test is SILENT: no conclusion, fall back to the first derivative test. (x⁴, -x⁴, and x³ all have f' = f'' = 0 at zero, with a min, a max, and neither, respectively — the silence is genuine.)

Worked on the running cubic f(x) = x³ - 3x² - 9x + 4: critical points -1 and 3; f''(x) = 6x - 6. f''(-1) = -12 < 0: local max at -1. f''(3) = 12 > 0: local min at 3 — matching the 1DT's verdicts from the sign chart, as it must.

2DT versus 1DT, the strategic comparison: 2DT is FASTER when f'' is easy and nonzero at the critical points — two evaluations replace a whole sign chart. 1DT is MORE GENERAL: it works when f'' is messy, when f''(c) = 0, and at critical points where f' is undefined (cusps — 2DT cannot even be stated there). Default: 2DT for clean polynomials and quick classification; 1DT when the second derivative resists or the test goes silent.

One more 2DT virtue: it needs only the VALUE f''(c), not intervals — making it the tool of choice for table problems ('f'(3) = 0 and f''(3) = -5; classify') and for implicit curves (evaluate the implicit y'' at the flat point). The exam writes both formats annually; the answer is one sentence: 'f'(3) = 0 and f''(3) < 0, so by the Second Derivative Test f has a local maximum at x = 3.'
key_terms: f' = 0 and f'' > 0: min; f'' < 0: max; f'' = 0: silent
x⁴ vs -x⁴ vs x³ — all silent cases, all different outcomes
2DT for clean evaluations; 1DT for cusps, messes, and silence
boxes: ap_alert

The 2DT sentence is two facts and a citation: 'f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) < 0, so by the Second Derivative Test, local max at c.' BOTH facts must be stated — omitting the f'(c) = 0 clause (the test's precondition) is a real deduction.

sections.title: The Full Sign-Chart Stack
sections.subtitle: f, f', f'' in one dashboard
sections.body:
The complete analysis stacks two sign charts: f' (increasing/decreasing, extremes at flips) above f'' (concavity, inflections at flips), aligned on one number line. The running cubic's dashboard: f' is + − + over critical points -1, 3; f'' is − + over the inflection candidate 2. Reading down columns gives the local shape on each stretch: rising-capped, falling-capped, falling-cupped, rising-cupped — the four taxonomy cells in sequence, with the curve's portrait now fully determined up to vertical placement.

The dashboard answers the AP's favorite cross-examination instantly. 'Where is f increasing AND concave down?' — read both rows: (-∞, -1). 'Where do f' and f'' agree in sign?' — columns with matching symbols. Such conjunction questions are lookups for chart-builders and nightmares for improvisers; the chart is the entire strategy.

Consistency checks live in the stack: between consecutive extremes there must be an inflection (a falling curve cannot start rising without un-bending somewhere), and a max must sit capped (f'' ≤ 0 nearby) while a min sits cupped. Violations in your charts mean an arithmetic error upstream — the dashboard self-audits.

Given GRAPHS instead of formulas, the same dashboard assembles from visual reads: f'-graph above/below axis fills row one; f'-graph rising/falling fills row two (since f'' is f''s slope). And given only a TABLE of f, f', f'' values at points, behavior questions reduce to citing the relevant signed value. Formula, graph, table — one dashboard, three input formats, every Unit 5 question type. Chapter 5 turns the dashboard into finished curve sketches.
key_terms: f' and f'' rows aligned on one number line — the analysis dashboard
'Increasing and concave down' reads two rows at once
Extremes need an inflection between them; maxes sit capped, mins cupped
boxes: ap_alert

Between any local max and the next local min, a continuous twice-differentiable curve MUST inflect — if your charts show two extremes with no inflection between, recheck the f'' row before submitting. The audit catches sign errors that feel invisible otherwise.

mcq.explanation: Flat tangent on a concave-down (capped) arc: a peak.
