choices.A: The Second Derivative Test gives no conclusion; use the First Derivative Test
choices.B: f has an inflection point at c
choices.C: f has no extreme at c
choices.D: f has a local minimum at c

mcq.explanation: Silence is silence: x⁴ (min), -x⁴ (max), x³ (neither) all fit these facts. Only a sign analysis of f' settles it.

mcq.question: The graph of f' has a local maximum at x = 4. The graph of f has
mcq.explanation: An extreme of f' is where f's slope stops rising and starts falling — concavity flips: inflection of f.

frq.question:
Let f(x) = x⁴ - 6x² + 8x + 1.
(a) Find f'(x) and f''(x), and verify that x = 1 is a critical point.
(b) Classify x = 1 using the Second Derivative Test if possible; if the test is silent, say so and classify with the First Derivative Test instead. (Note: f'(x) factors as f'(x) = 4(x - 1)²(x + 2).)
(c) Find all inflection points of f, verifying each sign change.
rubric: (b) f''(1) = 0: 2DT silent; 1DT with the factored f': (x-1)² keeps sign + around 1 (sign of (x+2) > 0): no sign change ⟹ no extreme at 1
(c) f'' = 12(x-1)(x+1): flips at both ±1
Inflections at (-1, f(-1)) = (-1, -12) and (1, f(1)) = (1, 4), changes verified
frq.model_answer: (a) f'(x) = 4x³ - 12x + 8 and f''(x) = 12x² - 12. f'(1) = 4 - 12 + 8 = 0 ✓. (b) f''(1) = 0 — the Second Derivative Test is silent. Using the factorization f'(x) = 4(x - 1)²(x + 2): near x = 1, (x + 2) > 0 and (x - 1)² ≥ 0, so f' is positive on both sides — no sign change, hence NO local extreme at x = 1 (the curve pauses while rising). (c) f''(x) = 12(x - 1)(x + 1): sign + − + across x = -1 and x = 1, changing at both. Inflection points: (-1, f(-1)) = (-1, 1 - 6 - 8 + 1) = (-1, -12) and (1, f(1)) = (1, 4).

frq.question:
A twice-differentiable function h satisfies: h'(2) = 0, h''(2) = 3; h'(5) = 0, h''(5) = 0; h'(8) = 0, h''(8) = -6. Additionally, h'(x) < 0 on (4, 5) and h'(x) > 0 on (5, 6).
(a) Classify the critical points x = 2 and x = 8, citing the appropriate test.
(b) Classify x = 5, explaining why the Second Derivative Test cannot do the job and what information rescues the classification.
(c) Must h have an inflection point in (2, 8)? Justify.
rubric: (a) x = 2: 2DT with h'' > 0 ⟹ local min; x = 8: h'' < 0 ⟹ local max
(b) h''(5) = 0: silent; the given h'-signs (− to +) give a local min by the 1DT
(c) Yes: h is capped at 8 (h'' < 0) and cupped at 2 (h'' > 0)
Applies the IVT to the continuous h'' on [2, 8]: h'' passes from positive to negative, so it vanishes and changes sign — an inflection of h
frq.model_answer: (a) At x = 2: h'(2) = 0 and h''(2) = 3 > 0, so by the Second Derivative Test h has a local minimum. At x = 8: h'(8) = 0 and h''(8) = -6 < 0: local maximum. (b) At x = 5, h''(5) = 0 — the 2DT is silent. But the problem supplies h' signs: negative on (4, 5), positive on (5, 6) — a − to + change, so by the First Derivative Test h has a local minimum at x = 5. (c) Yes. h''(2) = 3 > 0 and h''(8) = -6 < 0. If h'' is continuous (granted for AP purposes by twice-differentiability with the values given), the IVT applied to h'' on [2, 8] produces a point where h'' = 0 — and since h'' genuinely transitions from positive to negative values, a sign change (hence an inflection of h) occurs in (2, 8).

frq.question:
An epidemic's cumulative case count is modeled by a smooth increasing function C(t) whose graph is S-shaped: concave up on (0, 12), concave down on (12, 30), with C(12) = 4000.
(a) Interpret the point (12, 4000) in the language of this chapter and in plain English about the epidemic.
(b) The health ministry says 'cases are still rising, but the situation is improving' at t = 15. Translate into derivative signs and verify the claim's consistency with the model.
(c) On which day is the number of NEW cases per day greatest? Justify.
rubric: (a) (12, 4000) is the inflection point — concavity flips; epidemic's fastest-spread moment
(b) 'Still rising': C' > 0; 'improving': C'' < 0 (the growth rate is falling) — consistent with concave down at 15
(c) New cases per day = C'(t), maximized where C'' changes + to −: t = 12
Justification: C' increases on (0,12), decreases after — peak of C' at the inflection
frq.model_answer: (a) The point (12, 4000) is the inflection point of C: concavity switches from up to down there. Epidemiologically, day 12 is the day the outbreak's spread peaked — case counts still rise after it, but the daily increase starts shrinking. (b) 'Cases still rising' is C'(15) > 0; 'situation improving' is C''(15) < 0 — the growth rate itself is declining. The model agrees: t = 15 lies in the concave-down region, where C' > 0 (increasing function) and C'' < 0. (c) New cases per day IS C'(t). C' increases where C'' > 0 (on (0, 12)) and decreases where C'' < 0 (after 12), so C' peaks at t = 12 — the inflection day is the worst day for new infections, exactly why inflection points headline epidemic reporting.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: Curve Sketching — Connecting f, f', and f''
hook: Given a formula, you can now deduce where a curve rises, falls, bends, peaks, and flattens — without a calculator, without plotting points. Curve sketching is the unit's capstone proof that you understand what derivatives SAY, and the AP tests the connections in every direction.
learning_objectives: Assemble complete curve sketches from f, f', and f'' analysis
Incorporate asymptotes and end behavior into derivative-based portraits
Match graphs of f, f', and f'' to each other in any pairing
Translate between behavior tables and graphs in both directions
Diagnose inconsistencies between proposed graphs and derivative data

sections.title: The Sketching Protocol
sections.subtitle: Dashboard to drawing
sections.body:
The full protocol assembles everything the unit built: (1) domain, intercepts where cheap, and asymptotes/end behavior (Unit 1's limits); (2) f' analysis — critical points, sign chart, increasing/decreasing, classified extremes; (3) f'' analysis — concavity chart, inflection points; (4) plot the anchor points (extremes, inflections, intercepts) with their y-values; (5) connect with arcs matching each interval's (f' sign, f'' sign) cell from the 2×2 taxonomy.

Worked spine: f(x) = x³ - 6x² + 9x. Domain ℝ; intercepts x = 0, 3 (factoring x(x-3)²); end behavior −∞ to ∞. f' = 3(x-1)(x-3): + − + ⟹ rising to a max at (1, 4), falling to a min at (3, 0), rising away. f'' = 6x - 12: inflection at (2, 2), cap before, cup after. Anchors: (0,0), (1,4), (2,2), (3,0). Connect: rising-capped into (1,4), falling-capped to (2,2), falling-cupped to (3,0), rising-cupped away. The sketch draws itself.

The arc vocabulary is worth a moment's drill — four arc shapes for the four cells: rising-cupped (J-curve), rising-capped (climbing but tiring), falling-capped (over the top), falling-cupped (leveling out of a dive). Sketches assembled from correct arcs are unmistakable to graders even when drawn freehand.

What the AP actually asks: full sketches rarely; PIECES constantly. 'Find and classify extremes' is steps 2; 'find inflection points' is step 3; 'on which intervals is f increasing and concave up?' reads two charts at once. The protocol is the superset; every Unit 5 analytic question is a subset.
key_terms: Limits/asymptotes, f' chart, f'' chart, anchor points, taxonomy arcs
Extremes, inflections, and intercepts with computed y-values — the skeleton
Four arc shapes matching the four (f', f'') sign cells
boxes: ap_alert

When an FRQ says 'sketch a graph consistent with the table,' graders check: extremes at the right x-values, correct increasing/decreasing arcs between them, and concavity matching — NOT artistic quality. Anchor the named points, draw the right arc types, done.

sections.title: Asymptotic Portraits
sections.subtitle: Rational functions, fully analyzed
sections.body:
Rational functions add asymptote scaffolding to the protocol. f(x) = (x² - 4)/(x² - 1): vertical asymptotes where the (reduced) denominator vanishes — x = ±1; horizontal from the degree rule — y = 1 both directions. Sign analysis of f itself across the asymptotes and zeros (±2) frames which 'corridors' the curve occupies before any derivative is computed.

Derivatives then refine within corridors: f'(x) = 6x/(x² - 1)² (quotient rule, simplified). The squared denominator keeps f''s sign equal to the sign of 6x: falling for x < 0, rising for x > 0, within each domain piece. The single critical point is x = 0 with f(0) = (-4)/(-1) = 4 — and since the middle branch dives toward −∞ on both sides as x → ±1, the point (0, 4) is that branch's local maximum. Cross-checking each critical value against its corridor catches errors the algebra alone misses.

Slant asymptotes (degree gap one) integrate the same way: divide, sketch the line, and let the remainder term's sign show which side the curve hugs at each end. BC exams enjoy one rational-function analysis with a slant; the division is Unit 1.7's, the derivative work is this unit's.

The asymptote-aware protocol ordering matters: limits FIRST, derivatives second. Students who compute f' before mapping the asymptotes routinely classify extremes into corridors the curve never visits. Geography before topography.
key_terms: Regions between asymptotes and zeros where the curve's sign is fixed
Asymptotes and end behavior before derivative refinement
Divide, draw the line, sign the remainder to pick the hugging side
boxes: ap_alert

A critical point's classification must be consistent with its corridor: a 'local max' whose value sits below a corridor's floor signals an algebra error. The two-second value-vs-corridor sanity check is free insurance on rational-function questions.

sections.title: The Matching Game
sections.subtitle: f, f', f'' in any pairing
sections.body:
Graph-matching questions show two or three curves and ask which is f, which f', which f''. The decision rules, in order of power: (1) zeros of one curve must align with extremes of another (f' = 0 under f's peaks); (2) where one curve is positive, its antiderivative-partner must rise; (3) inflections of f align with extremes of f' and zeros of f''. Apply rule 1 to candidate pairs and most matchings collapse immediately.

Degree logic shortcuts polynomial matchings: differentiation drops degree by one, so the wiggliest curve (most turning points) is f, the next f', the flattest f''. A cubic-parabola-line trio matches by shape class alone. Trig matchings rotate phases: sine's derivative leads by a quarter period — the curve peaking where another crosses zero RISING is the derivative of the crosser.

The verification habit that prevents traps: after matching, spot-check ONE feature in each direction — 'f has a max at x = 2; does my f' cross zero downward there? f' has a min at 4; does my f'' cross zero upward there?' Thirty seconds, two checks, and the matching is bulletproof. Traps in these questions are mirror-images and sign-flips that survive sloppy matching but die under spot-checks.

Table-direction translations run the same correspondences without pictures: given a table of signs for f, f', f'' on intervals, select the consistent graph (or vice versa). The dashboard from last chapter IS the table; the protocol from this chapter IS the graph. The two formats are one analysis wearing different output devices.
key_terms: Zeros of f' under extremes of f; zeros of f'' under inflections of f
Most wiggles = f; each differentiation smooths one wiggle away
Verify one feature per pairing after matching — kills mirror traps
boxes: ap_alert

In matching questions, test EXTREME-to-ZERO alignment first — it eliminates wrong candidates fastest. Slope-reading ('this curve is positive so that one should rise') is the backup check, not the primary tool; it is slower and easier to fumble under pressure.

sections.title: Consistency Diagnosis
sections.subtitle: When data and graphs disagree
sections.body:
The inverse skill: given a proposed graph plus derivative data, find the inconsistency. 'The table says f'(3) = 0 and f''(3) > 0, but the graph shows a maximum at x = 3' — the 2DT demands a minimum; the graph is wrong. Diagnosis questions reward knowing the implications as two-way streets you can drive in REVERSE: every test that classifies also constrains.

The constraint catalog, assembled from the unit: extremes need f' sign changes (or endpoint status); maxima sit capped, minima cupped (when f'' exists and is nonzero); inflections need f'' sign changes; increasing intervals forbid downhill arcs; concave-up intervals demand the curve sit above its tangent lines. A proposed sketch violating any one is diagnosably wrong, and naming WHICH constraint broke is the answer.

MVT supplies the subtlest diagnostics: a table with f(1) = 3 and f(4) = 3 plus the claim 'f' > 0 on (1, 4)' is self-contradictory — Rolle forces a zero of f' between equal values. Average-rate bounds (MVT) catch impossible tables: f(0) = 0, f(2) = 10 with 'f'(x) ≤ 3 throughout' cannot coexist, since the average rate 5 must be attained. Theorems as lie detectors — the AP's most elegant question genre.

The unit closes where it opened: existence theorems (EVT, Rolle, MVT) plus classification machinery (1DT, 2DT, concavity) form one deductive system. Curve sketching exercises the system forward; consistency diagnosis exercises it backward; the exam exercises it in both directions, often in the same problem. Master the implications, not the rituals.
key_terms: Each test, read backward, forbids graph features — the diagnosis toolkit
Rolle/MVT expose impossible tables: equal values force zero rates; averages must be attained
Forward analysis and backward diagnosis are the same implications, both tested
boxes: ap_alert

'Which of the following could be the graph of f?' questions are elimination races: check each option against ONE strong constraint (usually extreme placement or concavity at a labeled point) and discard fast. Verifying the survivor fully beats verifying all options partially.

mcq.question: f'(x) > 0 and f''(x) < 0 on (2, 5). The graph of f on that interval is
mcq.explanation: Positive slope, negative bend: climbing but flattening — rising, capped.

mcq.question: f(x) = (x² - 4)/(x² - 1) has vertical asymptotes at
mcq.explanation: The denominator x² - 1 vanishes at ±1 with no cancellation (zeros are at ±2). y = 1 is the horizontal asymptote — a different feature.

mcq.question: Three graphs show a cubic, a parabola, and a line. If they are f, f', f'' in some order, then

choices.A: cubic = f, parabola = f', line = f''
choices.B: parabola = f, cubic = f', line = f''
choices.C: line = f, parabola = f', cubic = f''
choices.D: cubic = f, line = f', parabola = f''

mcq.explanation: Differentiation lowers polynomial degree by one: 3 → 2 → 1. Degree logic settles it without reading a single feature.

mcq.question: A table claims f(2) = 7, f(6) = 7, and f'(x) > 0 for all x in (2, 6). This data is

choices.A: impossible — Rolle's Theorem forces f'(c) = 0 somewhere in (2, 6)
choices.B: possible if f is concave up
choices.C: possible if f has an asymptote

mcq.explanation: Equal values at the ends of an interval where f is differentiable force a zero derivative between (Rolle) — 'always positive' contradicts it. (Implicitly f is differentiable since f' is discussed throughout.)

mcq.question: The graph of f'' is positive on (0, 3) and negative on (3, 7). Which feature does the graph of f have at x = 3?
mcq.explanation: f'' changes sign at 3: concavity flips, the definition of an inflection point. (Extremes of f need f' information, which is not given.)

frq.question:
Let f(x) = x³ - 3x² + 4.
(a) Find the intervals of increase/decrease and classify all extremes.
(b) Find the inflection point and the concavity intervals.
(c) Sketch-describe the curve: list the anchor points in order of x and name the arc type (rising/falling, cupped/capped) connecting each consecutive pair. Include end behavior.
rubric: (a) f' = 3x(x - 2): increasing on (-∞,0) and (2,∞), decreasing on (0,2); max at (0,4), min at (2,0)
(b) f'' = 6x - 6: inflection at (1, 2); concave down x < 1, up x > 1
(c) Anchors (0,4), (1,2), (2,0); arcs: rising-capped into (0,4), falling-capped to (1,2), falling-cupped to (2,0), rising-cupped away
End behavior: f → -∞ as x → -∞, f → ∞ as x → ∞
frq.model_answer: (a) f'(x) = 3x² - 6x = 3x(x - 2): positive, negative, positive across 0 and 2. Increasing on (-∞, 0) and (2, ∞); decreasing on (0, 2). Local max at (0, 4) (+ to −); local min at (2, 0) (− to +). (b) f''(x) = 6x - 6: negative before 1, positive after — inflection at (1, f(1)) = (1, 2); concave down on (-∞, 1), up on (1, ∞). (c) Coming from -∞ (end behavior of a positive cubic), the curve rises capped into the peak (0, 4); falls capped to the inflection (1, 2); continues falling but now cupped to the valley (2, 0); rises cupped toward +∞. Four arcs, four taxonomy cells, one S-shaped cubic.

frq.question:
Consider g(x) = x/(x² + 1).
(a) Explain why g has no vertical asymptotes, and find its horizontal asymptote(s).
(b) Find and classify all critical points.
(c) g has three inflection points. Find their x-coordinates. (g''(x) = 2x(x² - 3)/(x² + 1)³.)
rubric: (a) x² + 1 never zero: no VAs; degree rule: y = 0 both directions
(b) g' = (1 - x²)/(x² + 1)²: critical at ±1; min at (-1, -1/2), max at (1, 1/2)
(c) g'' zero at x = 0, ±√3, with sign changes at all three
Inflections at x = -√3, 0, √3
frq.model_answer: (a) The denominator x² + 1 ≥ 1 never vanishes, so no vertical asymptotes. Degrees: 1 below 2, so y = 0 is the horizontal asymptote in both directions. (b) g'(x) = ((x² + 1) - x(2x))/(x² + 1)² = (1 - x²)/(x² + 1)². Critical points x = ±1. Sign of g' is the sign of 1 - x²: negative, positive, negative — local min at (-1, -1/2), local max at (1, 1/2). (c) g''(x) = 2x(x² - 3)/(x² + 1)³ vanishes at x = 0, ±√3. The numerator 2x(x - √3)(x + √3) changes sign at each root (all simple), so all three are inflection points: x = -√3, 0, √3. The odd little curve rises from the axis, dips to -1/2, swings through the origin to +1/2, and settles back to the axis — with the bend flipping three times en route.

frq.question:
A student proposes a graph of a differentiable function h with these features: a local maximum at (2, 5); h decreasing on (2, 6); a local minimum at (6, 1); h concave down on the ENTIRE interval (0, 8).
(a) Use the unit's machinery to find the inconsistency in this proposal.
(b) State the theorem or test that exposes it.
(c) Repair the proposal minimally: change one feature so the description becomes consistent, and justify.
rubric: (a) A local min at 6 needs h' changing − to + (h rising just after 6), and a min sits cupped: h'' ≥ 0 nearby — contradicting concave down throughout
(b) The 2DT/concavity constraint (minima are cupped), or: between a max and a min, h' goes 0 → negative → 0, forcing h' to have a min, i.e., an inflection of h
(c) Repair: allow an inflection in (2, 6) — e.g., concave down on (0, 4), concave up on (4, 8)
Justification: the new concavity permits the cupped minimum at 6
frq.model_answer: (a) The proposal puts a local minimum at (6, 1) inside a region declared concave down. A minimum of a differentiable function is locally CUPPED: just after 6 the curve rises, and rising out of a valley requires the slope to increase through zero — h'' ≥ 0 near 6. Concave down on all of (0, 8) forbids exactly that. (b) The concavity constraint behind the Second Derivative Test exposes it (equivalently: h' falls from 0 at the max to 0 at the min, so h' must bottom out between — an inflection of h, impossible under single-signed h''). (c) Minimal repair: insert an inflection point — say h concave down on (0, 4) and concave up on (4, 8). Then the max at 2 sits capped (consistent), the curve un-bends at 4, and the min at 6 sits cupped (consistent). All other features survive untouched.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: What dimensions make the cheapest can, the largest pasture, the shortest cable? Optimization is calculus earning its keep in the real world — and on the AP, it's a word problem with a five-step skeleton that never changes.
learning_objectives: Translate verbal optimization problems into a function of one variable
Use constraint equations to eliminate variables before differentiating
Find and verify optima with the candidates test or derivative tests
Justify that a critical point is the requested extreme — the graded step
Solve the AP's classic scenarios: fencing, boxes, cans, distances, and costs

sections.title: The Optimization Skeleton
sections.subtitle: Objective, constraint, eliminate, optimize, verify
sections.body:
Every optimization problem runs one skeleton: (1) NAME the quantity to optimize and write its formula — the objective; (2) write the CONSTRAINT equation binding the variables; (3) ELIMINATE variables using the constraint until the objective has one variable, and state that variable's domain; (4) OPTIMIZE: find critical points of the single-variable objective; (5) VERIFY the candidate is the requested max/min and ANSWER the actual question asked.

The pasture classic: maximize the area of a rectangular field with 400 m of fence, one side along a river (unfenced). Objective: A = xy. Constraint: x + 2y = 400 (one x-side plus two y-sides). Eliminate: x = 400 - 2y, so A(y) = (400 - 2y)y = 400y - 2y², with domain 0 < y < 200. Optimize: A' = 400 - 4y = 0 at y = 100. Verify: A'' = -4 < 0 — a max. Answer: y = 100, x = 200, area 20,000 m².

Step 3's domain matters more than students expect: endpoints encode degenerate cases (zero-width fields), and on closed domains the candidates test needs them. When the domain is open, the verification step must argue the interior critical point wins — usually via the 2DT or the 1DT sign pattern.

Step 5's two halves both carry credit: the verification sentence (next section's subject) and answering the QUESTION ASKED — if the problem wants the minimum COST, report dollars, not the dimensions that achieve it. Re-read the question's last sentence before writing the final answer; optimization problems lose more points to mismatched answers than to wrong calculus.
key_terms: The quantity being maximized/minimized, as a formula
Solve the constraint for one variable, substitute into the objective
The eliminated objective's variable has physical bounds — state them
boxes: ap_alert

Write the objective and constraint as LABELED equations before any algebra: 'Maximize A = xy subject to x + 2y = 400.' The labeling sentence is setup credit on FRQs and the single best defense against optimizing the wrong quantity.

sections.title: The Justification Point
sections.subtitle: Proving your candidate is the winner
sections.body:
Finding the critical point earns partial credit; JUSTIFYING that it is the requested extreme earns the rest. The AP accepts three justification routes, each one sentence. Route A — Second Derivative Test: 'A''(y) = -4 < 0, so y = 100 gives a local maximum; as the only critical point in the domain, it is the absolute maximum.' Route B — First Derivative Test: 'A' > 0 for y < 100 and A' < 0 for y > 100, so A increases then decreases: absolute max at y = 100.' Route C — Candidates test (closed domains): the comparison table itself is the justification.

The 'only critical point' clause in Route A is load-bearing: a local max among several critical points might lose globally; a local max that is the ONLY critical point on an interval where the function is differentiable cannot be beaten (the function would need to come back up through another critical point). Examiners look for the clause; include it whenever it is true.

Route B's strength: it proves GLOBAL optimality directly — increasing-then-decreasing leaves no room for rivals. On open domains where endpoints cannot be checked, Route B (or A-plus-only) is the standard play. Route C is mandatory when endpoints are live candidates: a cost function on 1 ≤ r ≤ 5 might bottom out at r = 5.

Ungraded justifications that FEEL convincing but score zero: 'this is obviously the max,' 'the graph shows it,' plugging in two nearby points ('A(99) and A(101) are smaller'). Nearby-point checks prove local-ness at best; the rubric wants derivative-based reasoning. One sentence, one route, every time.
key_terms: Negative f'' plus 'only critical point in the domain' = absolute max
Increasing-then-decreasing proves the absolute claim directly
Closed domain: the comparison table is the justification
boxes: ap_alert

The justification is a dedicated rubric point on every optimization FRQ — historically the most-dropped point in Unit 5. Pre-write the three sentence templates in your head; on exam day, pick the matching route and transcribe.

sections.title: The Scenario Repertory
sections.subtitle: Boxes, cans, distances, and cost mixes
sections.body:
Open-top box from a sheet: cut squares of side x from the corners of a W×L sheet, fold. V(x) = x(W - 2x)(L - 2x), domain 0 < x < min(W,L)/2. Expand, differentiate, solve the quadratic in the domain. The cubic volume with quadratic derivative is the genre's fingerprint.

The cylindrical can: minimize surface area at fixed volume V₀. Objective S = 2πr² + 2πrh; constraint πr²h = V₀ eliminates h = V₀/(πr²): S(r) = 2πr² + 2V₀/r. S' = 4πr - 2V₀/r² = 0 gives r³ = V₀/(2π) — and substituting back, h = 2r: the optimal can is exactly as tall as it is wide. Real cans deviate for manufacturing reasons, an aside that makes the result memorable.

Closest-point problems: minimize the distance from (3, 0) to the parabola y = x². The move that saves algebra: minimize the SQUARED distance D = (x - 3)² + x⁴ — distance and its square share minimizers (squaring is increasing on nonneds), and the square root's chain rule fee vanishes. D' = 2(x - 3) + 4x³ = 0 — solve (here numerically or by inspection-friendly setups on the exam). Declare the squared-distance substitution; it is expected, not sneaky.

Cost mixtures: cable from an offshore platform to a coastal station — underwater segments cost more per mile than overland. Total cost C(x) = c₁√(x² + d²) + c₂(L - x) over the landing point x. C' = 0 balances the marginal costs; the solution typically satisfies a clean sine/ratio condition. These blend the distance template with economic weighting and are BC's favorite hard optimization.
key_terms: V = x(W-2x)(L-2x): cubic objective, quadratic derivative, bounded domain
Fixed volume, min surface ⟹ h = 2r — height equals diameter
Minimize D² instead of D: same winner, no square-root calculus
boxes: ap_alert

When minimizing any distance, write 'minimizing D² minimizes D since squaring preserves order on positive values' and work with D². The sentence licenses the simplification; the simplification halves the differentiation work.

sections.title: Optimization Judgment
sections.subtitle: Domains, units, and the reasonableness pass
sections.body:
Physical domains police the mathematics. Negative lengths, cut-squares larger than the half-sheet, probabilities beyond 1 — constraint violations masquerade as critical points whenever the algebra produces multiple roots. The domain stated in skeleton step 3 is the filter: discard out-of-domain critical points EXPLICITLY ('x = 7 is rejected since the domain is 0 < x < 4'), because the discard is part of the graded logic.

Units ride through optimization like every applied chapter: a maximized area answers in square meters, a minimized cost in dollars, and mixed-rate problems (cost per underwater mile versus overland) demand consistent units before any equation is written. The exam occasionally plants a feet/inches mismatch in the stem; the setup step is where to catch it.

The reasonableness pass after solving: does the optimal can's h = 2r look like a real can (roughly, yes)? Does the pasture use ALL the fence (it must — leftover fence means a bigger field was available)? Is the maximum-volume box's cut between zero and the half-width? Thirty seconds of plausibility checking catches sign errors, domain slips, and constraint misreads that survive the algebra.

Unit synthesis, closing the analytical arc: critical points (Ch 2) found by derivative rules (Units 2-3), classified by sign tests (Ch 3-4), assembled into portraits (Ch 5), now DEPLOYED on applied objectives. The remaining chapter extends behavior analysis to implicit curves — and then Unit 6 changes the question entirely, from slopes to accumulations.
key_terms: Out-of-domain critical points are discarded by name, as graded logic
Plausibility-check the optimum against the physical story
Optimal solutions use the full budget/fence/material — slack signals errors
boxes: ap_alert

If a quadratic derivative yields two roots, expect exactly one in the physical domain — and SAY why the other is rejected. Silent discards leave graders unsure you saw the issue; explicit discards convert a potential deduction into evidence of command.

mcq.question: A farmer has 240 m of fence for a rectangular pen against a barn (no fence on the barn side). The maximum area is
mcq.explanation: A(y) = (240 - 2y)y maximizes at y = 60, x = 120: area 7200 m².

mcq.question: Two nonnegative numbers sum to 20. The maximum value of their product is
mcq.explanation: P = x(20 - x) peaks at x = 10: P = 100.

mcq.question: To minimize the distance from the point (0, 3) to the curve y = x², the cleanest objective function is
mcq.explanation: Squared distance from (0, 3) to (x, x²): x² + (x² - 3)² — same minimizer as D, no radical. (D matches the wrong anchor point.)

mcq.question: An open-top box is made by cutting x-by-x squares from the corners of a 12-by-12 sheet. The domain of the volume function V(x) = x(12 - 2x)² is
mcq.explanation: The fold needs positive base width: 12 - 2x > 0 gives x < 6, with x > 0 for a positive height.

mcq.question: C(r) = 2πr² + 250/r for r > 0 (a can's cost). C'(r) = 4πr - 250/r². The justification that the critical point gives an absolute minimum is best stated as

choices.A: C'' = 8π + 500/r³ > 0 for all r > 0, and it is the only critical point
choices.B: C(r) is large at the critical point
choices.C: C(1) and C(5) are both bigger
choices.D: the graph looks like a valley

mcq.explanation: Positive second derivative everywhere (the function is convex) plus uniqueness of the critical point — Route A at full strength. B is meaningless; C proves only local comparisons; D is ungraded.

frq.question:
A rectangular poster must contain 600 cm² of printed area, with 5 cm margins top and bottom and 3 cm margins on each side. Let x be the WIDTH of the printed area.
(a) Express the total poster area A as a function of x alone, and state the domain.
(b) Find the dimensions of the printed area that minimize the total poster area.
(c) Justify that your answer gives the absolute minimum.
rubric: (a) Printed height = 600/x; A(x) = (x + 6)(600/x + 10), domain x > 0
(c) A'' = 7200/x³ > 0 for all x > 0 and unique critical point ⟹ absolute min
Final dimensions reported for the PRINTED area as asked
frq.model_answer: (a) The printed area is x wide and 600/x tall. The poster adds 3 cm margins each side and 5 cm top and bottom: A(x) = (x + 6)(600/x + 10) = 600 + 10x + 3600/x + 60 = 660 + 10x + 3600/x, for x > 0. (b) A'(x) = 10 - 3600/x² = 0 gives x² = 360, x = 6√10 ≈ 18.97 cm. Printed height: 600/x = 600/(6√10) = 10√10 ≈ 31.62 cm. The printed area should be 6√10 cm wide by 10√10 cm tall. (c) A''(x) = 7200/x³ > 0 for every x in the domain, so the objective is concave up throughout and x = 6√10, the only critical point, gives the absolute minimum total area.

frq.question:
A 10 dm³ (10,000 cm³) closed cylindrical drum is to be built. The material for the top and bottom costs 0.06 dollars/cm², and the side costs 0.04 dollars/cm².
(a) Write the cost as a function of the radius r alone.
(b) Find the radius minimizing the cost. (Leave the answer in exact cube-root form.)
(c) A consultant claims that at the optimal radius, the side costs exactly twice as much as the top and bottom combined. Verify or refute the claim using your optimal r.
rubric: (c) At the optimum 0.24πr³ = 800, so the ends cost 0.12πr² = 400/r while the side costs 800/r — ratio exactly 2
Concludes the claim is TRUE: side costs twice the ends at the optimum
frq.model_answer: (a) Volume: πr²h = 10000, so h = 10000/(πr²). Ends: 2πr² at 0.06 → 0.12πr². Side: 2πrh at 0.04 → 0.08πr·(10000/(πr²)) = 800/r. C(r) = 0.12πr² + 800/r, r > 0. (b) C'(r) = 0.24πr - 800/r² = 0 ⟹ r³ = 800/(0.24π) = 10000/(3π), so r = (10000/(3π))^{1/3} ≈ 10.2 cm. (C'' = 0.24π + 1600/r³ > 0 and the critical point is unique: absolute minimum.) (c) At the optimum, 0.24πr³ = 800, i.e. 0.12πr² = 400/r. The ends cost 0.12πr² = 400/r and the side costs 800/r — exactly twice. The claim is true: the optimal drum splits its budget 2:1 between side and ends, a fingerprint of the 0.04/0.06 price ratio.

frq.question:
A power station is on the bank of a straight river 300 m wide; a factory is 1000 m downstream on the opposite bank. Cable costs $5 per meter underwater and $3 per meter on land. The cable will run underwater from the station to a point P on the opposite bank x meters downstream, then on land from P to the factory.
(a) Write the total cost as a function of x, with domain.
(b) Find the value of x that minimizes the cost.
(c) Verify the minimum with a derivative test and compute the minimum cost.
rubric: Endpoint check or global argument included (closed domain: compare C(0) = 4500, C(1000) ≈ 5220)
frq.model_answer: (a) The underwater leg spans √(x² + 300²) = √(x² + 90000); the land leg is 1000 - x. C(x) = 5√(x² + 90000) + 3(1000 - x), 0 ≤ x ≤ 1000. (b) C'(x) = 5x/√(x² + 90000) - 3 = 0: 5x = 3√(x² + 90000), 25x² = 9x² + 810000, x² = 50625, x = 225 m. (c) C' < 0 for x < 225 and C' > 0 for x > 225 (the ratio 5x/√(...) increases with x), so C falls then rises: absolute minimum at x = 225, confirmed against the endpoints (C(0) = 5·300 + 3000 = 4500; C(1000) = 5√(1090000) + 0 ≈ 5220). Minimum cost: C(225) = 5√(50625 + 90000) + 3(775) = 5(375) + 2325 = 1875 + 2325 = $4200.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: Circles, ellipses, and folium curves don't pass the vertical line test — but they still have flat tops, steep sides, and bending arcs. This closing chapter points the unit's entire toolkit at curves that aren't functions, exactly the way the BC exam likes to.
learning_objectives: Find horizontal and vertical tangent points on implicit curves systematically
Determine concavity of implicit curves via implicit second derivatives
Classify points on implicit curves using sign analysis adapted to branches
Combine implicit differentiation with the unit's tests in FRQ-style sequences
Handle the dual-condition systems (derivative condition + original equation) cleanly

sections.title: Flat Tops and Steep Sides, Revisited
sections.subtitle: The two-equation systems
sections.body:
Unit 3 located horizontal tangents (numerator of dy/dx zero) and vertical tangents (denominator zero) on implicit curves. This unit's lens upgrades the question from WHERE to WHAT: a horizontal-tangent point on a closed curve is typically its highest or lowest point — a constrained extreme — and the locating system doubles as an optimization tool.

The ellipse x² + xy + y² = 12: dy/dx = -(2x + y)/(x + 2y). Horizontal candidates: y = -2x on the curve: x² - 2x² + 4x² = 12 gives x = ±2 — points (2, -4) and (-2, 4). Vertical candidates: x = -2y similarly gives (4, -2), (-4, 2). The four points frame the tilted ellipse: top at (-2, 4), bottom at (2, -4), rightmost (4, -2), leftmost (-4, 2). 'Find the highest point on the curve' is solved by the horizontal-tangent system — implicit optimization without ever isolating y.

The system discipline from Unit 3 persists: the tangent condition AND the original equation, solved simultaneously; candidates where both numerator and denominator vanish get flagged for special handling, not blind classification.

Why the exam loves this: it braids Unit 3 mechanics with Unit 5 interpretation in one problem — typically (a) find dy/dx, (b) locate the horizontal tangent points, (c) classify or interpret them. Parts (a) and (b) are computation; part (c) is this unit. The braid is the single most predictable BC implicit FRQ.
key_terms: Horizontal-tangent points are the curve's local tops and bottoms
Tangent condition + original curve, solved simultaneously
(a) dy/dx, (b) tangent points, (c) classification — the standard sequence
boxes: ap_alert

After solving the horizontal-tangent system, VERIFY the denominator is nonzero at each solution: a point killing both numerator and denominator is not a horizontal tangent but a singular point needing separate analysis. The one-line check ('at (2, -4), x + 2y = -6 ≠ 0 ✓') is graded.

sections.title: Concavity on Implicit Curves
sections.subtitle: y'' with the original equation recycled
sections.body:
Classifying an implicit curve's flat points needs concavity, and concavity needs the implicit second derivative — the Unit 3 workflow (differentiate y', substitute y', recycle the original equation) now serving the 2DT. The circle's y'' = -25/y³ classified its arcs; general curves run the same play with more algebra.

Efficient classification at a SPECIFIC flat point skips the general y'': differentiate the dy/dx expression (or the once-differentiated equation), then substitute the point's x, y, AND y' = 0 — the zero slope kills entire terms, collapsing the computation. On x² + xy + y² = 12 at (2, -4): differentiate 2x + y + (x + 2y)y' = 0 once more to get 2 + 2y' + (1 + 2y')y' + (x + 2y)y'' = 0. Setting y' = 0 at the flat point wipes out the middle terms: 2 + (x + 2y)y'' = 0, so y'' = -2/(x + 2y) = -2/(-6) = 1/3 > 0 — concave up: (2, -4) is the curve's LOW point. The y' = 0 collapse is the technique's entire speed advantage.

The matching classification at (-2, 4): by the same formula y'' = -2/(x + 2y) = -2/6 = -1/3 < 0 — concave down, the HIGH point. Symmetric curves often yield mirrored verdicts from one computation; noticing the symmetry halves the work and signals understanding in written solutions.

The 2DT's statement adapts verbatim: at a point with dy/dx = 0, positive y'' means a local minimum OF THE BRANCH through that point, negative a local maximum. The branch language matters — implicit curves carry several function-branches, and classification is per-branch. The exam's phrasing ('the curve has a local maximum at...') implicitly means the branch, and answering in branch terms is always safe.
key_terms: Substituting the flat point's zero slope before solving for y'' kills most terms
Implicit verdicts are per-branch: the arc through the point cups or caps
Symmetric curves yield mirrored classifications from one computation
boxes: ap_alert

At a horizontal-tangent point, differentiate the ONCE-differentiated equation and immediately set y' = 0 — never compute the general y'' formula first. The collapse turns a quotient-rule marathon into three lines, and BC FRQ rubrics are written expecting the short route.

sections.title: Full Behavior Analysis
sections.subtitle: A worked implicit dossier
sections.body:
The folium-style curve x³ + y³ = 6xy rewards a complete dossier. dy/dx = (2y - x²)/(y² - 2x) (Unit 3 computation). Horizontal tangents: x² = 2y on the curve. Substituting y = x²/2: x³ + x⁶/8 = 3x³, so x⁶ = 16x³ and x³ = 16, giving x = 2^{4/3} and y = x²/2 = 2^{8/3}/2 = 2^{5/3}. The arithmetic is heavier than the concept: one genuine flat point on the loop, at (2^{4/3}, 2^{5/3}). Vertical tangents mirror by the curve's x↔y symmetry: (2^{5/3}, 2^{4/3}).

The symmetry observation does real work: the folium is symmetric across y = x (swap x and y and the equation is unchanged), so every feature reflects — flat points pair with steep points, and one dossier entry generates its mirror for free. Exam curves are chosen with such symmetries; spotting them is both a checker and a shortcut.

Singular points — where numerator AND denominator of dy/dx vanish — get the flagged treatment: for the folium, (0, 0) kills both 2y - x² and y² - 2x. The origin is where the loop crosses itself: two branches, two tangent directions, no single slope. The AP handles singular points gently (usually 'explain why dy/dx is not defined'), and the honest answer names the 0/0 form and the geometric crossing.

The dossier's exam format: a sequence of parts walking exactly this analysis — derivative, tangent points, a classification, sometimes a singular-point comment. Each part feeds the next; an early algebra slip cascades. The defensive practice: carry EXACT values (2^{4/3}, not 2.52) so later parts substitute cleanly, and re-verify each located point ON the original curve before moving on.
key_terms: Derivative, flat/steep points, concavity verdicts, singularities — the complete file
Swap-invariant equations mirror every feature across y = x
Both parts of dy/dx vanish: branches cross, no single tangent exists
boxes: ap_alert

Re-verify located points against the ORIGINAL equation before classifying them — a candidate that fails the curve equation is an algebra-slip artifact, and classifying a phantom point compounds one error into three. The verification line is cheap; the cascade is not.

sections.title: The Unit in One Problem
sections.subtitle: Synthesis and the road to integration
sections.body:
A capstone composite, sketched: the curve x² - xy + y² = 9 (a tilted ellipse). (a) dy/dx = (y - 2x)/(2y - x). (b) Horizontal tangents: y = 2x on the curve gives 3x² = 9, x = ±√3 — points (√3, 2√3) and (-√3, -2√3). (c) Classify: differentiate-and-collapse with y' = 0 gives y'' = -2/(2y - x); at (√3, 2√3): y'' = -2/(3√3) < 0 — the high point. (d) The MVT-flavored finale some FRQs add: between the high and low points, the curve's branches must pass through every intermediate height — IVT on a parametrized arc.

Every move in that composite is a chapter of this unit: critical-point hunting (Ch 2) via implicit systems (Ch 7), classification by the adapted 2DT (Ch 4, 7), existence reasoning (Ch 1). The unit's deliverable is not seven techniques but ONE analytical fluency that reads any curve — explicit, implicit, or data-described — for its behavior.

What the toolkit cannot yet do: measure. How LONG is the arc between the flat points? How much AREA does the closed curve enclose? Slopes and shapes answer 'what does it look like'; the next unit's integral answers 'how much.' The derivative tells the curve's story pointwise; the integral adds it up.

Unit 6 opens with exactly that turn: accumulation, the definite integral, and the theorem — fundamental in name and in fact — that welds the two halves of calculus together. The analytical machinery built here stays loaded: optimization returns inside integral applications, concavity returns in error analysis, and the MVT returns wearing an integral costume. Nothing in this unit retires.
key_terms: One implicit curve exercising the unit's full toolkit in sequence
The unified skill: read behavior from derivatives in any presentation
From slope-questions to amount-questions — Unit 6's integral
boxes: ap_alert

BC implicit FRQs cascade: part (c) uses part (b)'s points and part (a)'s derivative. Budget time to VERIFY parts (a) and (b) before classifying in (c) — thirty seconds of checking beats propagating one slip through three scored parts.

mcq.question: For the curve x² + 4y² = 16, the points with horizontal tangent lines are
mcq.explanation: dy/dx = -x/(4y) = 0 at x = 0; the curve gives 4y² = 16, y = ±2.

mcq.question: On the curve x² + y² = 25, y'' = -25/y³. The arc through (0, -5) is

choices.A: concave up — the point is the circle's bottom
choices.B: concave down — the point is the circle's top

mcq.explanation: y'' = -25/(-125) = 1/5 > 0: cupped. The lowest point of the circle, consistent with dy/dx = 0 there.

mcq.question: For an implicit curve, dy/dx = (3y - x)/(y - 3x). A point where BOTH 3y - x = 0 and y - 3x = 0 hold is

choices.A: a singular point requiring separate analysis

mcq.explanation: 0/0 in the slope formula means no single tangent direction — typically a self-crossing. Neither tangent classification applies without deeper analysis.

mcq.question: At a point on an implicit curve where dy/dx = 0 and (by the collapse computation) y'' = -4/3, the branch through the point has
mcq.explanation: Flat tangent plus negative second derivative: capped — a local max of that branch, by the 2DT.

mcq.question: The curve x³ + y³ = 6xy is unchanged when x and y are swapped. If it has a horizontal tangent at (a, b), it must have
mcq.explanation: Reflection across y = x swaps the roles of horizontal and vertical: the mirrored point carries the mirrored (vertical) tangent.

frq.question:
Consider the curve x² + xy + y² = 12.
(a) Find dy/dx.
(b) Find all points where the curve has a horizontal tangent line, verifying the denominator condition.
(c) Using the collapse technique (substituting y' = 0 after differentiating again), classify each point from (b) as the branch's local maximum or minimum.
rubric: (b) y = -2x into the curve: 3x² = 12, x = ±2 → (2, -4), (-2, 4); checks x + 2y ≠ 0 at both
(c) Differentiating again with y' = 0: 2 + (x + 2y)y'' = 0 → y'' = -2/(x + 2y)
At (2,-4): y'' = 1/3 > 0 local min; at (-2,4): y'' = -1/3 < 0 local max
frq.model_answer: (a) Differentiating: 2x + y + x y' + 2y y' = 0, so dy/dx = -(2x + y)/(x + 2y). (b) Horizontal tangents need 2x + y = 0, i.e., y = -2x, on the curve: x² + x(-2x) + 4x² = 3x² = 12, x = ±2. Points: (2, -4) and (-2, 4). Denominator check: x + 2y = 2 - 8 = -6 ≠ 0 and -2 + 8 = 6 ≠ 0 ✓ — both are genuine horizontal tangents. (c) Differentiate 2x + y + (x + 2y)y' = 0 once more and set y' = 0 at the points: 2 + (x + 2y)y'' = 0, so y'' = -2/(x + 2y). At (2, -4): y'' = -2/(-6) = 1/3 > 0 — the branch cups: local minimum (the curve's lowest point). At (-2, 4): y'' = -2/6 = -1/3 < 0 — local maximum (the highest point).

frq.question:
The curve y³ - xy = 6 passes through (1, 2).
(a) Verify the point and find dy/dx at (1, 2).
(b) Determine whether the curve has any horizontal tangent points at all, and justify.
(c) Find the points where the curve has a VERTICAL tangent line. (The system is 3y² = x with the original equation.)
rubric: (a) 8 - 2 = 6 ✓; differentiating: 3y²y' - y - xy' = 0 → y' = y/(3y² - x); at (1,2): 2/11
(b) Horizontal needs y = 0; substituting y = 0 into the curve gives 0 = 6, impossible — no horizontal tangents
(c) 3y² = x into the curve: y³ - 3y³ = 6 → y³ = -3, y = -3^{1/3}, x = 3·3^{2/3}
Verifies numerator y ≠ 0 at the point — genuine vertical tangent
frq.model_answer: (a) Check: 2³ - (1)(2) = 8 - 2 = 6 ✓. Differentiate: 3y² y' - (y + x y') = 0, so y'(3y² - x) = y and dy/dx = y/(3y² - x). At (1, 2): dy/dx = 2/(12 - 1) = 2/11. (b) A horizontal tangent requires the numerator y = 0. But y = 0 in the curve equation gives 0 - 0 = 6 — impossible. The curve never crosses y = 0, and it has NO horizontal tangent points. (c) Vertical tangents: denominator zero, 3y² = x, substituted into the curve: y³ - (3y²)y = -2y³ = 6, so y³ = -3, y = -3^{1/3} ≈ -1.442, and x = 3y² = 3·3^{2/3} ≈ 6.24. At this point the numerator y ≠ 0, so the tangent is genuinely vertical: the point is (3·3^{2/3}, -3^{1/3}).

frq.question:
An elliptical track is modeled by 4x² + y² = 100 (units in meters).
(a) Find the coordinates of the track's northernmost point using calculus (not inspection), showing the horizontal-tangent system.
(b) Classify the point with an implicit second-derivative computation.
(c) A drone must hover over the track point with the steepest slope dy/dx in magnitude. Explain — using the vertical-tangent analysis — why no such 'steepest finite slope' point exists, and describe what happens to slopes near the track's east and west extremes.
rubric: (a) dy/dx = -4x/y = 0 → x = 0; curve: y² = 100 → northernmost (0, 10)
(b) Differentiate 8x + 2y y' = 0 again, set y' = 0: 8 + 2y y'' = 0 → y'' = -4/y = -2/5 < 0: local max ✓
(c) Slopes -4x/y blow up as y → 0 (points (±5, 0)); for any finite bound there are nearer points with larger slope
Describes |dy/dx| → ∞ approaching the east/west extremes — vertical tangents there
frq.model_answer: (a) Differentiating: 8x + 2y y' = 0, so dy/dx = -4x/y. Horizontal tangent: -4x = 0, x = 0; on the curve y² = 100, y = ±10. The northernmost point is (0, 10). (b) Differentiate 8x + 2y y' = 0 again: 8 + 2(y')² + 2y y'' = 0; at (0, 10) with y' = 0: 8 + 20 y'' = 0, y'' = -2/5 < 0 — concave down: a local maximum of the branch, confirming (0, 10) is the top. (c) The slope -4x/y grows without bound in magnitude as y → 0 along the curve — i.e., approaching the east and west extremes (±5, 0), where the tangents are vertical (denominator zero, numerator -4(±5) ≠ 0). For any candidate 'steepest finite slope' point, track points closer to (±5, 0) have steeper slopes still, so no maximum finite slope exists; the slopes increase without limit toward the vertical-tangent points.
